title: Steered Not Stirred: Effective Reward Tilting using Surrogate Reward Mixing

paper.title: Steered Not Stirred: Effective Reward Tilting using Surrogate Reward Mixing
paper.abstract: Abstract Continuous-time generative models, from diffusion models, flow matching, and now flow maps, owe their practical value to high-fidelity generation and steerability. In many applications, a ground-truth latent “oracle” reward R ∗ R^{*} is unavailable or expensive to evaluate, e.g., human judgments or experimental measurements. Although the oracle reward is not directly observable, it can often be approximated through multiple cheaper surrogates that, individually, provide incomplete characterizations but collectively reveal substantial information about the downstream task. In this paper, we present a method for composing such surrogates to steer a pretrained model toward the distribution tilted by an unavailable R ∗ R^{*} . Given a small feedback set of oracle rankings or numerical rewards, we introduce M ixing A nd R eward T ilting for IN ference-time I mprovement ( Martini ), which learns a surrogate composition for plug-and-play use with standard inference-time steering methods. Our theory characterizes surrogate information limits and relates population recovery error to ideal-target KL at small tilt strength. For preferences, the bound additionally accounts for an irreducible mismatch between the Plackett–Luce population target and the conditional mean. Experiments demonstrate improved oracle-tilt fidelity in language generation and ImageNet alignment, and improved joint pose accuracy and validity in protein–ligand cofolding, without inference-time oracle queries.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: In many real-world deployments, generative models are judged not only by sample fidelity to the pretraining distribution, but by whether their generations satisfy downstream task-specific objectives ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Consequently, it remains imperative to align generative models to desired rewards through algorithmic frameworks such as inference-time steering or post-training ( Uehara et al., 2025 ) that, in effect, sharpen the model distribution on samples with high downstream utility, where that utility is too costly or inaccessible to supervise at pretraining scale. The central discrepancy between pre-training and downstream task alignment, therefore, requires high-quality post-training data under an oracle reward, whose acquisition is often bottlenecked due to high collection costs ( Gao et al., 2023 ) , from capturing the nature of human preferences ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ; Ethayarajh et al., 2024 ) to experimental measurements needed to evaluate biomolecular design ( Pathak et al., 2025 ) . In lieu of carte blanche access to a reward oracle that is perfectly predictive of a desired downstream task, practitioners often have access to multiple weakly informative signals in the form of surrogate or proxy reward models. In text-to-image generation, for example, human preferences are approximated by aesthetic, alignment, and learned preference scores such as, ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) , CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , and PickScore ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) . In molecular and protein design, physical plausibility checks ( Buttenschoen et al., 2024 ) and machine-learned interatomic potentials ( Wood et al., 2025 ) similarly serve as proxies for physical assays or high-fidelity simulations. In each example, cheap proxy reward signals are individually imperfect and only weakly correlated with the true downstream task, yet collectively they contain substantial information and often complementary evidence for successful candidates. Despite this promise—including the potential to mitigate reward hacking ( Coste et al., 2024 ; Eisenstein et al., 2023 ) —existing inference-time steering methods for diffusion and flow-matching models are largely formulated around a single surrogate reward. As a result, a key missing development is a principled framework for composing multiple proxies to recover the latent oracle objective, rather than standard multi-objective optimization that treats surrogates as separate objectives. This motivates a fundamental question: How can multiple weak reward surrogates be composed to steer a pretrained diffusion or flow model towards the reward-tilted distribution favored by an unavailable oracle? \tikzscale@endList \tikzscale@endList Figure 1: Martini learns a surrogate composition g ∘ 𝐑 g\circ\mathbf{R} from limited offline oracle feedback and uses it to steer toward q g q_{g} , aiming to approximate the gold reward tilt q ∗ q^{*} . At inference, Martini steers without querying R ∗ R^{*} . Present work . We study steering toward the reward-tilted distribution of a latent oracle reward, R ∗ R^{*} , available only on a small annotated feedback set, using multiple cheap surrogates and no query access to R ∗ R^{*} at inference. More precisely, we formulate two settings representative of real-world use, in which the feedback set supplies either preference rankings over candidate samples or direct scalar reward values. We introduce Martini ( M ixing A nd R eward T ilting for IN ference-time I mprovement, Figure 1 ), which learns a composition of the surrogates from that feedback and allows plug-and-play deployment in existing reward steering frameworks. Martini exploits complementary surrogate information to improve steering toward R ∗ R^{*} , targeting a different solution concept from Pareto optimization. We summarize our main contributions as follows: 1. Methods . We develop a novel algorithm in Martini that exploits the problem structure of steering towards a gold reward R ∗ R^{*} , witnessed only on a feedback set, by learning a composition function over cheap reward surrogates that can readily interface with existing steering pipelines. 2. Theory . We characterize the information limit of the surrogates and identify the exact KL-optimal composition. Conditional-mean regression minimizes recovery error and the leading small-guidance KL coefficient. We also bound reward gain and gap, and relate preference fitting to these quantities through the discrepancy between its population target and the conditional mean. 3. Results . We evaluate Martini on language generation, ImageNet text alignment, and protein–ligand cofolding, as well as toy experiments, spanning FKS ( Singhal et al., 2025 ) , FMRG ( Huang et al., 2026 ) , MFM ( Potaptchik et al., 2026 ) , and Itô steering ( Pan et al., 2026 ) methods.

sections.heading: 2.2 Preference modelling
sections.text: Preference learning aims to fit a latent utility h h from relative rankings rather than scalar-valued scores (as in, e.g., regression tasks), by minimizing a negative log-likelihood (NLL). The Bradley–Terry (BT) model ( Bradley and Terry, 1952 ) models pairwise rankings p ⁡ ( x i ≻ x j ) = σ ⁡ ( h ⁡ ( x i ) − h ⁡ ( x j ) ) p(x_{i}\succ x_{j})=\sigma(h(x_{i})-h(x_{j})) , with σ \sigma the logistic sigmoid function. The Plackett–Luce (PL) model ( Plackett, 1975 ; Luce, 1959 ) extends this to a full ranking π \pi of a candidate set S S of size m m , decomposed into a sequence of softmax choices over the items not yet selected, p PL ​ ( π ∣ h , S ) = ∏ i = 1 m − 1 exp ⁡ ( h ⁡ ( x π ⁡ ( i ) ) ) / ∑ i ′ = i m exp ⁡ ( h ⁡ ( x π ⁡ ( i ′ ) ) ) p_{\mathrm{PL}}(\pi\mid h,S)=\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}\exp(h\left(x_{\pi(i)}\right))\big/\sum_{i^{\prime}=i}^{m}\exp\left(h\left(x_{\pi(i^{\prime})}\right)\right) , recovering BT at m = 2 m=2 and is invariant to additive constants. Such models are pervasive in LLM post-training: annotators rank responses to a prompt, and the goal is to align the model to human judgements of quality using RL or direct preference optimization ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Rafailov et al., 2023 ) .

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: Martini learns a composition of fixed surrogates from an offline feedback set 𝒟 feedback {\mathcal{D}}_{\text{feedback}} , distinct from the generator’s training data 𝒟 train {\mathcal{D}}_{\text{train}} . Feedback consists of numerical oracle rewards or rankings; the fitted composition drives inference-time steering without oracle queries.

sections.text: We evaluate Martini on language generation, text-to-image alignment, and protein–ligand cofolding, fitting g g offline and steering without inference-time oracle queries, with synthetic experiments in § I . Evaluation . For language and images, we assess recovery using held-out PCC and MSE for values, or SCC and PL loss for preferences. Experimental tilts use the sampler law p 1 , ϕ p_{1,\phi} in place of p 1 p_{1} . We evaluate fixed finite target tilts β = 1 \beta=1 and sweep sampler guidance separately, probing behavior beyond our small- β \beta guarantees. sections.heading: 4.3 Protein-Ligand Co-folding
sections.text: Protein–ligand cofolding provides a setting with experimental scalar feedback. We ask whether a surrogate composition learned from binding-affinity measurements can improve the accuracy and physical validity of the jointly generated poses. Qualitative results shown in Figure 3 (right) and Figure 21 . Setup . Using the value regime, we fit a composition of five surrogates to experimental p ​ K D \mathrm{p}K_{D} measurements from HiQBind ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , restricting the feedback set to PoseBusters-valid monomers and multimers ( Buttenschoen et al., 2024 ) . We evaluate on 186 186 complexes from the post-2023 subset of Runs N’ Poses ( Škrinjar et al., 2026 ) , beyond Boltz-1’s training cutoff. As these evaluation complexes lack measured affinities, we assess transfer through pose accuracy and physical validity, reporting best@1 metrics averaged over five seeds. Dataset filtering, surrogate definitions, and steering details are in § F . Metrics . Our success rate is the percentage of predictions with RMSD below 2 2 Å that pass PoseBusters validity checks ( Buttenschoen et al., 2024 ) . We also report accuracy and validity rates alongside lDDT-PLI , which measures local protein–ligand distance agreement within a 6 6 Å pocket ( Mariani et al., 2013 ) , as well as structural diversity detailed in § F.3 . sections.heading: 5 Related work
sections.text: Reward-based control . Generative models can be aligned through reinforcement learning ( Black et al., 2024 ) or preference optimisation ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ; Wallace et al., 2024 ; Bai et al., 2026 ) , and steered at inference through guidance ( Bansal et al., 2023 ; Singhal et al., 2025 ) , posterior sampling ( Chung et al., 2023 ) , or flow-map optimal control ( Huang et al., 2026 ) . Martini complements these methods by learning the steering reward from offline oracle feedback. Reward compositions and limited feedback . Reward ensembles can mitigate over-optimisation ( Coste et al., 2024 ) . ReNO uses fixed reward weights ( Eyring et al., 2024 ) , while SLOP calibrates pooled scores to maximize estimated gold reward ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . We study approximation of a fixed oracle tilt from values or rankings, characterizing the information limit imposed by the surrogates. Multi-objective methods balance distinct rewards ( Ramé et al., 2023 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) . Limited oracle access also motivates query-efficient fine-tuning ( Uehara et al., 2024 ) , protein steering ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , and optimisation over generated samples ( Willis et al., 2025 ) . We use feedback to learn how fixed surrogates predict a single oracle, keeping the generator unchanged. Complementing analyses of proxy error and ensembling ( Paes et al., 2026 ) , we relate fitting loss and surrogate information limits to steering fidelity and reward bounds.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Martini learns surrogate compositions offline from oracle values or rankings for reuse across compatible steerers without inference-time oracle queries. Our theory links fitting to ideal-tilt fidelity and reward improvement, identifying surrogate information limits and conditions for useful steering despite imperfect recovery. Experiments demonstrate benefits across language, images, and protein–ligand cofolding. KL and reward expansions are local in β \beta , with larger tilts assessed empirically. Preference guarantees require convex, range-bounded classes, and their tightness remains unassessed. Robustness beyond synthetic PL rankings remains untested. ImageNet guidance uses per-pair reference energy, leaving selection without oracle-scored references an open task.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: Steering pretrained generative models, including language models, can amplify biases or errors in the base model, oracle, or surrogate rewards, and can generate harmful content. Improvements in measured reward do not establish safety, fairness, or factual correctness. Likewise, computational protein–ligand metrics do not replace experimental validation. Applications require task-specific evaluation and appropriate safeguards.

sections.text: We consider correlation weighting, linear compositions, and MLPs. Linear and MLP compositions minimize the value or preference loss in Equations 3 and 4 , with regularization. sections.heading: B.1 ImageNet
sections.text: We use the released model of Potaptchik et al. [2026] ( mfm-xl2 ), a SiT-XL/2 transformer distilled from the Decoupled MeanFlow ImageNet model [ Lee et al., 2026b ] . It generates class-conditional ImageNet images at 256 × 256 256\times 256 in the latent space of the Stable Diffusion VAE ( sd-vae-ft-mse ; latents of shape 4 × 32 × 32 4\times 32\times 32 , scaled by 0.18215 0.18215 ), with noise at t = 0 t=0 , data at t = 1 t=1 and the linear interpolant x t = ( 1 − t ) ​ ε + t ​ x 1 x_{t}=(1-t)\varepsilon+t\,x_{1} . The model is conditioned only on the ImageNet class label: the text prompt never enters the model, and acts only through the rewards — R ∗ R^{*} and the surrogates score the decoded image against it. Reward models . The oracle uses Skywork/Skywork-VL-Reward-7B . The four surrogates are RE-N-Y/hpsv21 , RE-N-Y/ImageReward , openai/clip-vit-base-patch16 , and yuvalkirstain/PickScore_v1 . For each image and steering prompt, the oracle score is the Yes/No logit margin, R ∗ ​ ( x ) = logit Yes ​ ( x ) − logit No ​ ( x ) . R^{*}(x)=\mathrm{logit}_{\mathrm{Yes}}(x)-\mathrm{logit}_{\mathrm{No}}(x). Target . q ∗ ∝ p 1 , ϕ ​ exp ⁡ ( β ​ z ​ ( R ∗ ) ) q^{*}\propto p_{1,\phi}\exp(\beta z(R^{*})) , β = 1 \beta=1 , is estimated by self-normalised reweighting of 8192 8192 independent draws from the model’s reverse SDE ( 32 32 steps); the effective sample size of these weights is reported per class in Table 4 . Feedback and fitting . ImageNet uses n = 32 n{=}32 scalar R ∗ R^{*} evaluations (value) or M = 128 M{=}128 ranking queries of m = 8 m{=}8 candidates each (preference), drawn from the class’s pool. We fit separate composition coefficients for each class–prompt pair. A fifth of the value labels ( 6 6 ) and a quarter of the preference queries ( 32 32 , built from images disjoint from the fitting queries) are held out; every family is fit on the remainder, and the family is selected by held-out MSE (value) or Plackett–Luce loss (preference), averaged over all 19 19 pairs. The linear family is selected in both regimes. The held-out part is used only for this selection and is not refit. loss. Preference utilities . The synthetic annotator sorts z ⁡ ( R ∗ ) + σ ​ ϵ z(R^{*})+\sigma\epsilon with independent standard Gumbel noise ϵ \epsilon and σ = 0.5 \sigma=0.5 , which samples Plackett–Luce rankings with utilities z ⁡ ( R ∗ ) / σ z(R^{*})/\sigma . We standardise R ∗ R^{*} once over the reference pool, fixing its scale across queries. In our eight-candidate calibration (a standard-normal oracle), σ = 0.5 \sigma=0.5 gives 82.7 % 82.7\% pairwise agreement with the unperturbed oracle order. This noise level is loosely informed by the approximately 81 % 81\% non-tie human agreement reported on MT-Bench [ Zheng et al., 2023 ] ; agreement with an oracle order and agreement between annotators are different quantities. A fitted utility f f is expressed in PL units, so the tilt it implies on the reference scale is exp ⁡ ( β ​ σ ​ f ) \exp(\beta\sigma f) . In practice we standardise the fitted composition over the pool before use, so the steering reward and KL g \mathrm{KL}_{g} both use exp ⁡ ( β ​ z ​ ( f ) ) \exp(\beta z(f)) , which coincides with exp ⁡ ( β ​ σ ​ f ) \exp(\beta\sigma f) when f f recovers the utility exactly. Pools and data splits . For each class–prompt pair and feedback regime, we draw an independent pool of 8192 8192 samples and score the oracle and surrogates. Within each regime, the pool supplies feedback candidates, normalization statistics, and the importance-weighted reference § C . Held-out recovery is measured on pool rows that no fit or selector touched, subsampled to at most 4000 4000 . Oracle and surrogate scores are computed once per pool sample and cached. The prior p 1 , ϕ p_{1,\phi} is 64 64 fresh draws from the FMRG sampler at zero strength, and BoN, sBoN and SLOP select from an independent pool of 4096 4096 such draws, never from the reference they are scored against; these rows come from a separate run with its own 8192 8192 -draw reference. Steering and strength selection . We use FMRG for ImageNet and sweep its guidance strength λ ∈ { 2 , 3 , 5 , 8 } \lambda\in\{2,3,5,8\} separately from the target tilt strength β = 1 \beta=1 . Each run takes 32 32 kernel transitions with a reward-gradient step after each, the reward evaluated on one look-ahead endpoint (one noise draw, one flow-map jump), and each setting is a single run of 64 64 samples, scored afresh. For each method and class–prompt pair, all generated-sample metrics are reported at the evaluated strength with the lowest embedding-space energy distance to q ∗ q^{*} . This selection uses the oracle-scored reference and describes performance within the evaluated sweep. Baselines . BSS is selected from training feedback via either PCC or SCC for value and preference regimes respectively. Uniform weighting combines the normalized surrogate scores with equal weights. For images, ReNO uses its published fixed reward weights within the same FMRG pipeline [ Eyring et al., 2024 ] . This compares reward mixtures rather than reproducing ReNO’s original noise-optimization procedure. We also compare ParetoFlow [ Yuan et al., 2025 ] and SLOP’s calibrated selection protocol [ Wang et al., 2026 ] . SLOP is calibrated using numerical oracle values; its preference-regime results are therefore a value-calibrated reference. BoN selects the highest- R ∗ R^{*} candidate among N N candidates, requiring N N oracle evaluations per output.

sections.heading: B.2 Language generation
sections.text: We use the released FMLM checkpoint [ Lee et al., 2026a ] ( david3684/FMLM-B-LM1B ), trained on One Billion Words [ Chelba et al., 2013 ] . Generation is unconditional, with 128 128 tokens from the 30,522 30{,}522 -token bert-base-uncased vocabulary generated in 8 8 flow-map steps, at softmax temperature 1 1 and without per-step noise injection ( γ = 0 \gamma=0 ). We use FMRG steering and feedback budgets of n = 256 n=256 numerical rewards or M = 256 M=256 rankings of m = 8 m=8 candidates, labelled by the same Plackett–Luce annotator as ImageNet ( σ = 0.5 \sigma=0.5 ). Each evaluated setting is run with 5 5 seeds of 256 256 generated samples; metrics are computed per seed and averaged, and | gap | |\mathrm{gap}| is taken from the seed-averaged mean. The oracle is negative per-sequence generative perplexity under Qwen2.5-1.5B [ Qwen et al., 2025 ] , scored in fp32 after removing the [CLS] separators that LM1B’s sentence packing leaves inside each sample. The surrogates are unmasked pseudo-log-likelihoods from BERT and DistilBERT ( bert-base-uncased , distilbert-base-uncased ; the mean log-probability the MLM head assigns to each token actually present, in a single forward pass without masking), a CoLA acceptability score (the acceptable-minus-unacceptable logit margin of textattack/bert-base-uncased-CoLA ), and the empirical unigram entropy of the sample. All four share the generator’s vocabulary, so their differentiable extensions read a distribution over tokens directly: it is multiplied into each scorer’s word-embedding matrix (between the [CLS] and [SEP] embeddings), and the entropy is taken of the position-averaged distribution. On one-hot inputs these reduce exactly to the discrete scores. Held-out loss selects an MLP for values and a linear composition for preferences. Pools and steering . For each run, 2048 2048 unsteered samples are scored by the oracle and all surrogates: 1536 1536 rows supply the feedback and 512 512 are held out for recovery, and the whole pool, importance-weighted, forms the q ∗ q^{*} reference (ESS 1155 1155 of 2048 2048 ). FMRG follows each flow-map step with two unit-normalised reward-gradient steps, x ← x + λ ​ ∇ x r / ∥ ∇ x r ∥ x\leftarrow x+\lambda\,\nabla_{x}r/\lVert\nabla_{x}r\rVert , where r r is evaluated on the endpoint prediction X t , 1 ​ ( x ) X_{t,1}(x) — one call of the two-time denoiser, on the vocabulary simplex — at every step. The strength grid is λ ∈ { 0.00375 , 0.0075 , 0.015 , 0.03 , 0.06 , 0.125 , 0.25 , 0.5 , 1 , 2 , 4 } \lambda\in\{0.00375,0.0075,0.015,0.03,0.06,0.125,0.25,0.5,1,2,4\} ; figures and tables show λ ≤ 0.125 \lambda\leq 0.125 , where the methods separate. Candidates may recur across ranking queries, so the M = 256 M=256 groups contain 2048 2048 candidate occurrences rather than 2048 2048 distinct samples.

sections.heading: F.1 Surrogates
sections.text: We fit the surrogate composition to experimental binding-affinity feedback and evaluate its transfer to generated structures. The five surrogates provide information about structural quality, binding-site energetics, and predicted affinity. SMINA . SMINA is a widely used docking and scoring tool forked from AutoDock Vina and optimised for high-throughput scoring and for user-specified scoring functions [ Koes et al., 2013 ] . Frustration . The FrustratometeR R package Rausch et al. [2021] is used to calculate local energetic frustration in protein structures, where high frustration relates to unstable local regions and correlates with active sites. MolProbity . MolProbity [ Chen et al., 2010 ] assesses the physical quality of molecular structures through all-atom steric contact analysis with explicit hydrogens, together with covalent-geometry and backbone and side-chain torsion-angle criteria. Boltz Affinity . The boltz affinity prediction head introduced in Passaro et al. [2025] is used here as an affinity surrogate. The Boltz-2 weights are used to featurise the complex, but the pose itself is taken as atomic coordinates from the steering run (e.g. with DeCAF) and then used to constrain the affinity prediction, so that the prediction head uses the steered poses. Default Boltz-2 settings were used for this surrogate. Boltz-1x physical potentials. We include the physical potential terms used by Boltz-1x [ Wohlwend et al., 2025 ] to penalize stereochemical violations, clashes, and inconsistent chain geometry. The resampling coefficients are symmetric_chain_com 0.5 connections 1.0 posebusters 0.1 chiral 1.0 stereo 1.0 planar 1.0 vdw_overlap { 0.01 , t < 0.6 , 0 , t ≥ 0.6 . \begin{array}[]{lc}\texttt{symmetric\_chain\_com}&0.5\\ \texttt{connections}&1.0\\ \texttt{posebusters}&0.1\\ \texttt{chiral}&1.0\\ \texttt{stereo}&1.0\\ \texttt{planar}&1.0\\ \texttt{vdw\_overlap}&\begin{cases}0.01,&t<0.6,\\ 0,&t\geq 0.6.\end{cases}\end{array} Here t t is the resampling-time variable used by the implementation. These seven terms include both within-chain and between-chain contributions. We normalize the surrogate reward values both for fitting g g and during steering. Figure 8 displays the correlation of the surrogate rewards with the experimental HiQBind p ​ K D \mathrm{p}K_{D} as well as the theoretical recovery ceiling when using these surrogate rewards. SMINA is the best single surrogate based on the Pearson correlation. Boltz energy potentials are instrumental in ensuring physical validity of the generated poses; therefore, each baseline includes normalized energy potentials. \tikzscale@endList \tikzscale@endList Figure 8: Correlation of HiQBind scores with the experimentally measured binding affinity values The theory ceiling in Figure 8 is ρ info = 1 − v ¯ / Var ⁡ ( R ∗ ) \rho_{\mathrm{info}}=\sqrt{1-\bar{v}/\mathrm{Var}(R^{*})} , the highest PCC any function of the scores can reach, where v ¯ = 𝔼 ⁡ [ Var ⁡ ( R ∗ ∣ 𝐑 ) ] \bar{v}=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Var}(R^{*}\mid\mathbf{R})] is the variance of the measured affinity that the HiQBind scores leave unexplained, estimated by leave-one-out local-linear k k -nearest-neighbour regression of R ∗ R^{*} on 𝐑 \mathbf{R} .

sections.heading: F.2 Feedback and evaluation datasets
sections.text: HiQBind . HiQBind is a curated protein–ligand binding dataset constructed by matching experimentally determined binding free energies from BioLiP, Binding MOAD, and BindingDB to co-crystallized PDB complexes and reprocessing each entry through the open-source HiQBind-WF workflow [ Wang et al., 2025b ] . The release comprises 18,160 PDB entries with binding-affinity annotations and 32,275 refined non-covalent complexes, annotated with affinity values, release year, resolution, ligand and protein identifiers, and derived ligand properties. We subset this data set to monomers and multimers that have experimental p ​ K D \mathrm{p}K_{D} , leaving us with N=7095 for the feedback set. Runs N’ Poses. We evaluate on 186 186 complexes from the post-2023 subset of Runs N’ Poses [ Škrinjar et al., 2026 ] , beyond Boltz-1’s training cutoff. These evaluation complexes lack experimental affinity labels, so we measure pose accuracy and physical validity. This tests whether a composition fitted to affinity feedback transfers to structure generation; it does not directly measure recovery of the experimental affinity tilt. Avishek Joey Bose 2 2 footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: University of Cambridge Imperial College London Mila--Québec AI Institute Abstract Continuous-time generative models, from diffusion models, flow matching, and now flow maps, owe their practical value to high-fidelity generation and steerability. In many applications, a ground-truth latent “oracle” reward R ∗ R^{*} is unavailable or expensive to evaluate, e.g., human judgments or experimental measurements. Although the oracle reward is not directly observable, it can often be approximated through multiple cheaper surrogates that, individually, provide incomplete characterizations but collectively reveal substantial information about the downstream task. In this paper, we present a method for composing such surrogates to steer a pretrained model toward the distribution tilted by an unavailable R ∗ R^{*} . Given a small feedback set of oracle rankings or numerical rewards, we introduce M ixing A nd R eward T ilting for IN ference-time I mprovement ( Martini ), which learns a surrogate composition for plug-and-play use with standard inference-time steering methods. Our theory characterizes surrogate information limits and relates population recovery error to ideal-target KL at small tilt strength. For preferences, the bound additionally accounts for an irreducible mismatch between the Plackett–Luce population target and the conditional mean. Experiments demonstrate improved oracle-tilt fidelity in language generation and ImageNet alignment, and improved joint pose accuracy and validity in protein–ligand cofolding, without inference-time oracle queries. 1 Introduction In many real-world deployments, generative models are judged not only by sample fidelity to the pretraining distribution, but by whether their generations satisfy downstream task-specific objectives ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Consequently, it remains imperative to align generative models to desired rewards through algorithmic frameworks such as inference-time steering or post-training ( Uehara et al., 2025 ) that, in effect, sharpen the model distribution on samples with high downstream utility, where that utility is too costly or inaccessible to supervise at pretraining scale. The central discrepancy between pre-training and downstream task alignment, therefore, requires high-quality post-training data under an oracle reward, whose acquisition is often bottlenecked due to high collection costs ( Gao et al., 2023 ) , from capturing the nature of human preferences ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ; Ethayarajh et al., 2024 ) to experimental measurements needed to evaluate biomolecular design ( Pathak et al., 2025 ) . In lieu of carte blanche access to a reward oracle that is perfectly predictive of a desired downstream task, practitioners often have access to multiple weakly informative signals in the form of surrogate or proxy reward models. In text-to-image generation, for example, human preferences are approximated by aesthetic, alignment, and learned preference scores such as, ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) , CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , and PickScore ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) . In molecular and protein design, physical plausibility checks ( Buttenschoen et al., 2024 ) and machine-learned interatomic potentials ( Wood et al., 2025 ) similarly serve as proxies for physical assays or high-fidelity simulations. In each example, cheap proxy reward signals are individually imperfect and only weakly correlated with the true downstream task, yet collectively they contain substantial information and often complementary evidence for successful candidates. Despite this promise—including the potential to mitigate reward hacking ( Coste et al., 2024 ; Eisenstein et al., 2023 ) —existing inference-time steering methods for diffusion and flow-matching models are largely formulated around a single surrogate reward. As a result, a key missing development is a principled framework for composing multiple proxies to recover the latent oracle objective, rather than standard multi-objective optimization that treats surrogates as separate objectives. This motivates a fundamental question: How can multiple weak reward surrogates be composed to steer a pretrained diffusion or flow model towards the reward-tilted distribution favored by an unavailable oracle? 	ikzscale@endList 	ikzscale@endList Figure 1: Martini learns a surrogate composition g ∘ 𝐑 g\circ\mathbf{R} from limited offline oracle feedback and uses it to steer toward q g q_{g} , aiming to approximate the gold reward tilt q ∗ q^{*} . We study steering toward the reward-tilted distribution of a latent oracle reward, R ∗ R^{*} , available only on a small annotated feedback set, using multiple cheap surrogates and no query access to R ∗ R^{*} at inference.
